composition.story: A bill starts with one member of Congress. It moves through committee and a floor vote in each chamber. Both chambers must approve identical text. Then the President signs it, and it becomes law.

aha.observation: A bill becomes law only after the House and Senate both pass identical text and the President signs it.

states.label: Introduce
states.sentence: A member of Congress introduces the bill in the House.
states.why: Every bill needs a sponsor in one chamber.

states.label: House committee
states.sentence: A House committee studies, amends, and votes on whether to report the bill.
states.why: Most bills die here without a report.

states.label: House vote
states.sentence: The full House debates the bill and passes it by majority vote.
states.why: The first chamber has approved the text.

states.label: Senate committee
states.sentence: The bill moves to a Senate committee for the same review and amendment.
states.why: The Senate reviews the bill independently.

states.label: Senate vote
states.sentence: The full Senate debates the bill and passes it by majority vote.
states.why: The second chamber has approved a version.

states.label: Match text
states.sentence: If versions differ, the chambers reconcile them until both pass identical text.
states.why: Differing wording means no single bill can go forward.

states.label: President
states.sentence: The bill goes to the President, who may sign it or veto it.
states.why: A veto stops the bill unless two-thirds of each chamber override.

states.label: Law
states.sentence: The President signs. Both chambers agreed on identical text, so the bill is now law.
states.why: Two chamber approvals plus a signature complete the path.
